title: Unilateral Nonconfluent Cluster of Micronodules: Atypical Radiologic Appearance of Pulmonary Tuberculosis in an Immunocompetent Patient
case_text:
A 65-year-old immunocompetent man presented to the respiratory clinic with recurrent chronic productive cough and gradual loss of weight for 2 years. He denied any fever, haemoptysis, urinary symptoms, or contact to any patients with pulmonary tuberculosis. His initial vital signs were unremarkable (blood pressure = 130/70 mmHg, pulse rate = 76 beats per minute, oxygen saturation = 98% at room air, and temperature = 36.5 C). At the first encounter, he was underweight with a BMI of 17 kg/m2. On examination, there was reduced air entry in the left upper lung. The abdomen was soft and nontender. His sputum sample was sent for tuberculosis workup; however, the results were negative. Routine blood investigations including full blood count and urine profile were within normal limits. The inflammatory makers were not elevated with a white cell count of 11 g/dL. His past medical history included benign prostatic hyperplasia and remote history of healed scrotal abscess.
The initial chest radiograph revealed fibrotic lung changes in the upper zones, more so on the left than the right. Subsequently, a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the thorax with high-resolution CT reconstruction was performed and showed extensive scarring in both apical regions, again more so on the left. In addition, there were nonconfluent clusters of micronodules (Figure 1) in the right lung with a few smaller regions of tree-in-bud nodularity. There was no significant mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. In the upper part of the abdomen included in the CT, there were also incidental findings of the partial duplex system of the left kidney with mild-to-moderate hydronephrosis in the lower moiety with proximal hydroureter (Figure 2). To further investigate this urinary finding, a multiphasic renal CT scan was then performed and did not reveal any calculus, suspicious ureteric mass or external compression from lymphadenopathy. The culture of his urine sample grew mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) complex, and he was diagnosed with active genitourinary and pulmonary tuberculosis. He was commenced on antituberculous medication (Akurit-4). His symptoms improved, and he started to gain weight. A repeated CT scan at 4 months revealed significant improvement of the aforementioned clusters of micronodules, tree-in-bud changes, and left hydronephrosis. Given the positive urine culture for tuberculosis with concurrent respiratory and constitutional symptoms, and improvement of the lung changes and respiratory symptoms following antituberculous treatment, the above-described nonconfluent clusters of micronodules were likely to represent active pulmonary tuberculosis.

distillation_prompt.system_prompt:
You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: active genitourinary and pulmonary tuberculosis
